opus-5.5.text:
I think the most fundamental reason is that it opens up a new dimension of scaling. For the past few years, what we've mostly been doing is next-token prediction on ever larger amounts of data. That paradigm has been incredibly successful, but it runs into a real constraint: high-quality natural data is finite. The internet only has so much, and much of the most valuable stuff, the actual thinking process behind a good proof or a good piece of code, was never written down. People write down the final answer, not the hundred failed attempts that led there.

What o1-style models show is that you can let the model generate its own thinking process and use reinforcement learning to shape it. So instead of only scaling pre-training compute, you can scale compute at test time, letting the model think longer, try things, reflect, backtrack. And you can scale the RL itself, so the model learns from its own trajectories rather than relying purely on human-written data. In a sense, the model starts producing data that didn't exist before. I think that's a big shift, because it addresses the data bottleneck from a different angle.

The second reason is about what kinds of problems these models can solve. Before, a lot of the capability was like System 1, fast and intuitive pattern matching. That works for many tasks, but for math, competitive programming, or complex multi-step planning, you need something closer to System 2: deliberate, long-horizon reasoning where you can catch your own mistakes. Once the model learns behaviors like "wait, this doesn't look right, let me check again," the ceiling on hard reasoning tasks goes up dramatically. You see it in the benchmarks, but more importantly you see it in the quality of the process.

And third, I think it changes how we think about the roadmap toward more general intelligence. If you believe the end goal involves agents that can complete long, complex tasks on their own, then the ability to reason over long contexts, decompose problems, and self-correct is a prerequisite. Long chain-of-thought reasoning is kind of the foundation for that. So for us, it's not just one more feature on a model. It's a change in the paradigm of how capability gets created: from imitating human data toward learning through exploration and feedback. That's why I'd put it among the most important developments of the past year.

r001.rationale: The response says o1-style models can “try things, reflect, backtrack,” clearly describing repeated attempts within the reasoning process.

fable-5.1.text:
I think o1 matters because it changes the fundamental question of where scaling comes from. For the past few years, the whole field was running on one recipe: more data, more parameters, more compute in pretraining. That worked remarkably well, but everyone could see the ceiling approaching. High-quality human text is finite. You can keep adding parameters, but you can't manufacture another internet.

What o1 showed is that there's a second axis. You can scale compute at inference time, and you can scale reinforcement learning on top of the pretrained model, and both of those produce real gains in capability. That's not a small engineering trick. It means the model is no longer limited to imitating what humans have already written. Through RL, it can generate its own trajectories, explore, make mistakes, get a signal, and improve. In a sense, the model starts producing its own data, and that breaks the dependence on the natural data ceiling.

The second reason I think it's important is what it says about the nature of intelligence. Before, a lot of the capability was essentially recall and pattern completion. Very fast, very fluent, but if the answer wasn't somewhere in the distribution, the model struggled. With long chain-of-thought, the model gets to search. It can try a path, notice it's wrong, back up, try another one. That's much closer to what we mean when we say someone is thinking. And once you have that, difficulty stops being a hard wall. A problem that used to be impossible becomes a matter of how much thinking you're willing to spend.

And the third thing, which I find quite exciting, is that this generalizes beyond math and code. People initially saw o1 as a math model. But math and code are just the domains where verification is easy, so they're the natural place to start. The underlying capability, the ability to reason for a long time and self-correct, is general. As we figure out how to build reward signals for softer domains, I expect the same approach to lift writing, research, planning, agentic tasks, everything.

So from my perspective, it's not just a better model. It opened a new scaling paradigm when the old one was starting to feel saturated, and that's why I'd put it among the most important developments of the year.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can try a path, notice when it is wrong, back up, and try another, clearly describing repeated attempts within reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the important change is that we’re giving models another way to improve: spending more computation on a problem before producing an answer. Previously, a lot of progress came from scaling training—more data, more parameters, more compute. Models like o1 suggest that computation at inference time can also be a meaningful axis of scaling.

That matters because different problems require different amounts of thought. If you ask a simple factual question, you want an immediate answer. But for a difficult math problem or a complex coding task, it can be valuable for the model to explore an approach, check intermediate results, and revise its solution. The goal isn’t simply to produce a longer response; it’s to use that additional computation to reach a better answer.

There’s also an important connection to reinforcement learning. In areas where we can verify whether an answer is correct, we can train a model toward successful problem-solving without having to prescribe every step. That creates opportunities to go beyond imitating the reasoning examples people have written down.

Of course, the big question is how broadly this works, especially on tasks where correctness is harder to evaluate. But I regard it as important because it opens up a new path for improving foundation models, alongside scaling pretraining.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can explore an approach, check intermediate results, and revise its solution, conveying repeated attempts within its reasoning process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key development is that we now have another way to scale intelligence. Previously, we focused mainly on training: increasing the amount of data, the model size, and the compute used to train it. With models like o1, you can also spend more compute when answering a question, allowing the model to reason through a problem before giving its final answer.

That matters because some problems are difficult to solve in a single pass. You need to try an approach, examine whether it works, and perhaps take a different direction. If a model can learn that process, additional computation at inference time can translate into better answers.

I see this as an important new direction for foundation models. The question becomes not only how much knowledge a model has learned, but also how effectively it can use computation to solve a new problem. Of course, spending more time thinking is only useful if the reasoning is reliable, so improving that relationship is a central challenge.
